lead: Paul ends the oldest of his letters with a string of short commands for a young community: respect those who labour among you, rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks, do not quench the Spirit. In Mark, Jesus explains the parable of the sower: one word falls on four kinds of hearers. Read together, the two readings show what good soil looks like in a parish: people who receive the word with joy, keep it through trouble, and let it bear fruit in prayer, thanksgiving and patience with one another.

set: Thessalonica was the chief city of Macedonia. Paul founded the church there on his second missionary journey and had to leave the city in haste (Acts 17:1–10). He wrote this letter from Corinth, probably about AD 50, and most scholars hold it to be the oldest writing in the New Testament. The community was only a few months old.

Our passage comes at the very end of the letter, just before the closing blessing. After teaching about the Lord's coming (4:13–5:11), Paul gathers his practical counsel into short lines that are easy to remember.
str: vv. 12–13: respect and love for those who lead and labour in the community; peace among all.
vv. 14–15: care for the idle, the fainthearted and the weak; no repaying evil for evil.
vv. 16–18: rejoice, pray, give thanks: three commands and one reason, the will of God in Christ.
vv. 19–22: the Spirit and prophecy: do not quench, do not despise, test, hold fast, abstain.
kw: those who have charge of you

Literally “those who stand before” you. Paul uses the same word for those who lead in Romans 12:8. Within some twenty years of the Resurrection the young Church already had recognised leaders, and Paul asks that they be loved “because of their work”.
Without a break, kept up steadily. Paul uses the same word of his own constant remembering and thanksgiving for this church (1:3; 2:13). He asks of them what he already does for them.
The verb from which the word Eucharist comes. Thanksgiving “in all circumstances” is the habit of a people whose central act of worship is itself a thanksgiving.
vv: Peace in a community is the first fruit of respect for those who serve it.
See that none of you repays evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to all.
“And to all”: kindness does not stop at the church door. Paul echoes the Lord's own teaching (Matthew 5:44; compare Romans 12:17).
Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
People often ask what God's will is for them. Here is one clear answer, and it fits every state of life.
The image is of fire (compare Acts 2:3). The gifts of the Spirit can be put out by neglect or by contempt.
but test everything; hold fast to what is good;
ch: The Second Vatican Council turns to this passage when it speaks of the gifts of the Spirit: those who lead the Church must judge them, not to extinguish the Spirit, but to test all things and hold fast to what is good (Lumen Gentium 12, citing 1 Thessalonians 5:12, 19–21). The Catechism takes “pray constantly” as a description of the Christian life itself (CCC 2742). St Augustine, writing to the widow Proba, explains how this is possible: we pray without ceasing when we go on desiring, in faith, hope and love, the life that God alone can give (in substance).

set: Jesus has told the parable of the sower from a boat to the crowd on the shore (4:1–9). When he is alone with the Twelve and those around him, they ask him about the parables (4:10–12). Now he explains this one, and he treats it as the key to the others: the kingdom comes as a word sown, and everything depends on how it is received.
The explanation moves from the seed to the people. The seed on the path becomes “the ones on the path”. Each kind of ground is a kind of hearer.
str: v. 13: a question to the disciples: if they miss this parable, how will they understand the rest?
v. 14: the sower sows the word.
v. 15: the path: Satan takes the word away at once.
vv. 16–17: rocky ground: joy without root; trouble makes them fall away.
vv. 18–19: thorns: cares, wealth and desires choke the word.
v. 20: good soil: they hear, accept and bear fruit.
kw: In Mark the word is the Gospel message itself (compare 2:2, “he was speaking the word to them”). The first Christians called their preaching simply “the word” (Acts 8:4).
From skandalon, a trap or a stumbling block. Trouble and persecution become a trap that trips them, because there is no root to hold them.
Apatē means deceit. Wealth promises more than it can give, and so it deceives.
vv: Jesus does not stop to describe the sower. In the parable the seed falls everywhere, even where a careful farmer would not throw it. God is generous with his word.
But they have no root, and endure only for a while;
Joy is good, but joy without roots does not last. Roots grow out of sight: in prayer, in the sacraments, in the slow habits of faith.
but the cares of the world, and the lure of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it yields nothing.
Thorns do not kill quickly. They grow up beside the good plant until it has no light.
they hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.
Three verbs: hear, accept, bear fruit. The harvest is far beyond what anyone expected from so much seed that seemed wasted.
ch: St Gregory the Great, preaching on this parable, said that people would hardly believe him if he called riches thorns; yet they are thorns, because they tear the mind with their cares and do not let it rest (in substance). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the word of God is the strength of faith and the food of the soul for the Church's children (Dei Verbum 21). In every Holy Qurbana the word is sown before the Bread of life is given.

qa: Is the parable saying that some people are simply bad soil?

No. The four kinds of ground can be found in one heart, and at different times in one life. The path can be broken up and the thorns pulled out. The parable is a warning and an invitation, not a sentence passed on anyone.
study: Paul asks the community to love those who labour among them. Whom in my parish do I need to thank, or to pray for, this week?
Which of the four kinds of ground best describes my heart this Easter season, and what one thorn do I need to pull out?
